1

Fast Recap

Reconfirm the core SL ideas before you move into grouped reporting.

Reference pattern — multi-table retrieval recap 
SELECT a.column_a, b.column_b
FROM first_table AS a
INNER JOIN second_table AS b
    ON a.primary_key = b.foreign_key
WHERE a.status_column = 'HL'
ORDER BY b.name_column;

SELECT s.name_column, c.course_column, e.value_column
FROM junction_table AS e
INNER JOIN student_table AS s
    ON e.student_id = s.student_id
INNER JOIN course_table AS c
    ON e.course_id = c.course_id;

HL reporting still depends on clean joins. If the join path is wrong, the grouped result will also be wrong.

  1. A3.2.4 Composite key

    Identify the composite primary key in ENROLLMENT and explain what real-world relationship that table stores.

  2. A3.3.2 JOIN

    Join COURSE to DEPARTMENT and show each course with its department name and credit value.

  3. A3.3.2 JOIN 3 tables

    Show student full name, course name, and score for all Spring enrollments.

2

Aggregates and Grouped Reporting

Build reporting queries that summarize many rows into decision-making information.

Reference pattern — COUNT, AVG, SUM, MAX, MIN, GROUP BY, HAVING 
-- Count rows in each group
SELECT group_column, COUNT(*) AS row_count
FROM table_name
GROUP BY group_column;

-- Average a numeric value in each group
SELECT group_column, AVG(score_column) AS average_score
FROM table_name
GROUP BY group_column;

-- Total a numeric value in each group
SELECT category_column, SUM(number_column) AS total_value
FROM table_name
GROUP BY category_column;

-- Filter grouped results after aggregation
SELECT group_column, COUNT(*) AS row_count
FROM table_name
GROUP BY group_column
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 4;

COUNT, AVG, SUM, MAX, and MIN work on grouped data. HAVING is the clause that filters those grouped summaries.

  1. A3.3.4 COUNT

    Count how many courses each department offers.

  2. A3.3.4 COUNT

    Count how many enrollment rows each course has.

  3. A3.3.4 AVG

    Calculate the average score for each department.

  4. A3.3.4 MAX / MIN

    Return the maximum and minimum score in each course.

  5. A3.3.4 SUM

    Sum the course credits by level so you end up with one total for SL and one total for HL.

  6. A3.3.4 HAVING

    Show only departments with at least four enrollments.

  7. A3.3.4 Report query

3

Views

Create a reusable query layer on top of the base tables.

Reference pattern — CREATE VIEW 
CREATE VIEW useful_view AS
SELECT a.column_a, b.column_b, c.score_column
FROM first_table AS a
INNER JOIN link_table AS c
    ON a.primary_key = c.first_id
INNER JOIN second_table AS b
    ON c.second_id = b.primary_key
WHERE c.score_column >= 90;

SELECT *
FROM useful_view
ORDER BY score_column DESC;

A virtual view stores the query, not a second copy of the data. It can simplify long joins and hide unnecessary complexity from users.

  1. A3.3.5 CREATE VIEW

    Create a view called HighScorers that shows student full name, course name, department name, and score for rows where the score is at least 90.

  2. A3.3.5 Query a view

    Query HighScorers and order the result by score descending, then by student surname.

  3. A3.3.5 Explain

    Explain one benefit of a virtual view and one difference between a virtual view and a materialized or snapshot view.

4

Transactions and ACID

Use transaction control language to protect data integrity while changes are being made.

Reference pattern — BEGIN TRANSACTION, COMMIT, ROLLBACK 
BEGIN TRANSACTION;

INSERT INTO parent_table (id, name_column)
VALUES (9001, 'New record');

INSERT INTO child_table (parent_id, item_id, score_column)
VALUES (9001, 501, 88);

COMMIT;

BEGIN TRANSACTION;
UPDATE child_table
SET score_column = 91
WHERE parent_id = 9001;
ROLLBACK;

Use COMMIT when all related changes should become permanent together. Use ROLLBACK when you need to undo the whole transaction.

  1. A3.3.6 BEGIN / COMMIT

    Begin a transaction, insert a new student, insert one matching enrollment row for that student, then commit the transaction.

  2. A3.3.6 BEGIN / ROLLBACK

    Begin a second transaction, change a score or cohort value, inspect the result, then roll the transaction back.

  3. A3.3.6 ACID

    Explain how atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability help keep this database reliable when several changes happen close together.

Model Answers — Course Enrolment

Section 1

1
Recap answer ENROLLMENT has the composite key (StudentID, CourseID), representing which student is enrolled on which course.

Section 2

2
Aggregate examples 
SELECT d.DepartmentName, COUNT(*) AS EnrollmentCount
FROM ENROLLMENT AS e
INNER JOIN COURSE AS c
    ON e.CourseID = c.CourseID
INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT AS d
    ON c.DepartmentID = d.DepartmentID
GROUP BY d.DepartmentName
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 4;

Section 3

3
View pattern 
CREATE VIEW HighScorers AS
SELECT s.FirstName, s.LastName, c.CourseName, d.DepartmentName, e.Score
FROM ENROLLMENT AS e
INNER JOIN STUDENT AS s
    ON e.StudentID = s.StudentID
INNER JOIN COURSE AS c
    ON e.CourseID = c.CourseID
INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT AS d
    ON c.DepartmentID = d.DepartmentID
WHERE e.Score >= 90;

Section 4

4
ACID summary Atomicity keeps related changes together, consistency preserves valid states, isolation stops overlapping transactions from interfering, and durability keeps committed work safe after failure.
